item.title: Artemis II Flight Day 6: Lunar Flyby Updates - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Artemis II Flight Day 6: Lunar Flyby Updates

Live lunar flyby updates for NASA’s Artemis II mission will be published on this page. All times are Eastern.

9:35 p.m.

The Artemis II crew has completed the mission’s lunar observation period and is now beginning the return trip home. On Tuesday, April 7, Orion will exit the lunar sphere of influence at approximately 1:25 p.m., at a distance of 41,072 miles from the Moon.

8:35 p.m. 

Artemis II is now entering a solar eclipse that will last for about an hour as Orion, the Moon and the Sun align. During this phase, the crew will see the Sun disappear behind a mostly darkened Moon.

The crew will use the opportunity to study the solar corona — the Sun’s outermost atmosphere — as it glows around the lunar edge. They also will watch for flashes of light from meteoroids striking the surface, which could offer insight into potential hazards on the Moon.

7:24 p.m.

The Artemis II crew witnessed an Earthrise as Orion emerged from behind the Moon, moments before the Deep Space Network reacquired the spacecraft’s signal and restored communications.

7:02 p.m. 

The Artemis II crew has reached the mission’s maximum distance from Earth at 252,756 miles, setting a new record for human spaceflight. This milestone places the crew 4,111 miles farther from Earth than the Apollo 13 mission in 1970.

7:00 p.m. 

Orion has reached its closest approach to the Moon at about 4,067 miles above the lunar surface. At this point, the spacecraft is traveling about 60,863 miles an hour relative to Earth, but only 3,139 miles an hour relative to the Moon.

6:44 p.m.  

Victor Glover

Artemis II Pilot

The Orion spacecraft has entered a planned communications blackout as it passes behind the Moon. For about 40 minutes, the lunar surface blocks the radio signals from NASA’s Deep Space Network on Earth needed to stay in contact with the crew.

Similar blackouts occurred during the Artemis I and Apollo missions and are expected when using an Earth-based communications system. Once Orion emerges from behind the Moon, the network will quickly reacquire the signal and restore communications with mission control.

6:41 p.m.  

As Orion traveled behind the Moon, the crew witnessed an “Earthset” — the moment Earth dropped below the lunar horizon — marking another milestone in the mission’s lunar flyby.

The Earth will re-emerge at “Earthrise” from the opposite edge of the Moon in about 40 minutes.

4:40 p.m.

A lively stream of science observations from the crew throughout the flyby has been received with grins, nods, and lots of chatter in the Science Evaluation Room, where lunar scientists are supporting the observations in mission control. The crew reported color nuances, which will help enhance scientific understandings of the Moon. Shades of browns and blues that can be picked out with human eyes can help reveal the mineral composition of a feature and its age. As crew reports are received, the science team is updating the observation plan based on their follow up questions and sending up new guidance to the crew.

2:45 p.m.

Due to last approximately seven hours, the lunar observation period is the duration of time that the crew is close enough to the Moon to make impactful science observations (4,070 miles altitude at closest approach) and the spacecraft is oriented such that the windows are pointed at the Moon.

At the beginning of the window, as Orion approaches the Moon on the near side, the side we can see from Earth, people in parts of the eastern hemisphere can view some of the same features the astronauts will observe. These include future CLPS landing site Reiner Gamma, a bright, mysterious swirl the origin of which scientists are still trying to understand, and Glushko, a bright, 27-mile-wide crater known for the white streaks that shoot out from it for up to 500 miles.

1:56 p.m. 

The Artemis II crew of NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, along with CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen have set the record for the farthest distance from Earth traveled by a human mission, surpassing the Apollo 13 record of 248,655 miles set in 1970.

Jeremy Hansen

Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Astronaut and Artemis II Mission Specialist

NASA Flight Director Brandon Lloyd, Capsule Communicator Amy Dill, and Command and Handling Data Officer Brandon Borter also marked a lighthearted milestone today by emailing the crew what is now assumed to be the longest person-to-person message ever sent in human history.

After breaking the record for human spaceflight, crew also took a moment to provisionally name a couple of craters on the Moon, noting they were able to see them with their naked eye.

Just northwest of Orientale basin highlighted above is a crater they would like to name Integrity after their spacecraft and this historic mission. Just northeast of Integrity, on the near and far side boundary, and sometimes visible from Earth, the crew suggested Carroll crater in honor of Reid Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll Taylor Wiseman. After this mission is complete, the crater name proposals will be formally submitted to the International Astronomical Union, the organization that governs the naming of celestial bodies and their surface features.

1:30 p.m. 

NASA’s lunar science officer briefed the crew on their science objectives for the upcoming lunar observation period.

On April 5, the science team sent the crew the final list of 30 lunar surface targets, including the Orientale basin, a nearly 600-mile-wide crater that straddles the Moon’s near and far sides. This 3.8-billion-year-old crater formed when a large object struck the lunar surface and retains clear evidence of that collision, including dramatic topography in its rings. The crew will study Orientale’s features up close and from multiple angles as they pass by.

Hertzsprung basin also is on the crew’s list of targets. Northwest of Orientale, it is a nearly 400-mile-wide crater on the Moon’s far side. An older ringed basin, Hertzsprung offers a unique contrast to Orientale because its features have been degraded by subsequent impacts. By comparing the topography of the two craters, the crew’s observations will help scientists gain insight into how lunar features evolve over geologic timescales.

1 p.m.

NASA’s live coverage of the Artemis II lunar flyby is underway on NASA+, Amazon Prime, Apple TV, Hulu, Netflix, HBO Max, and Roku, alongside the agency’s 24/7 coverage on its YouTube channel. Learn how to stream NASA content through a variety of online platforms, including social media.

Coverage will include live views of the Moon from cameras mounted on Orion’s solar arrays. Image and view quality may vary throughout the lunar observation period due to distance from Earth, system limitations, and bandwidth across NASA’s communications network.

Note: The spacecraft will enter a planned communications blackout from 6:44 to 7:25 p.m. EDT as Orion passes behind the Moon. Spacecraft camera views will not be available during this time, but NASA’s live coverage will continue. 

View the latest imagery from the Artemis II mission on our Artemis II Multimedia Resource Page. Please follow @NASAArtemis on X, Facebook, and Instagram for real-time updates. Live coverage of the mission is available on NASA’s YouTube channel.

item.title: How NASA's elite recovery teams intercepts returning astronauts - USA Today
item.description:
How NASA's elite recovery teams intercepts returning astronauts

In April, after the Artemis II did a lap around the Moon to validate the Orion spacecraft and human deep-space systems for future lunar surface missions, the four astronauts aboard returned to Earth. But for some mission-critical members of the team, the work was just getting started.

After splashdown, NASA and a team of Navy divers needed to recover the four-person crew from the middle of the Pacific Ocean, which was no small feat. A lot can go wrong while retrieving the crew, and NASA plans for every contingency, no matter how remote.

“If we have a boat that fails, this is what we’re going to do. If we have high season conditions, this is what we’re going to do,” says NASA Artemis Landing and Recovery Director Liliana Villarreal. There are all sorts of back-up plans, Villarreal says, and thankfully none of them were needed.

Legacy of Apollo

The ocean recovery of Artemis II revives the legacy of the Navy frogmen and recovery divers who pulled Apollo crews from the sea beginning in the 1960s.

In planning for Artemis II’s return to Earth, NASA leaders had lengthy conversations with many of the personnel who worked on the Apollo missions. “They talked to them about lessons learned, and a lot of the things that went right in Apollo we've actually continued to use,” sVillarreal says.

While much was learned in the Apollo missions, “sometimes that tribal knowledge wasn’t documented,” she says. “It’s really good to be able to talk to the experts.”

Some things have changed since the Apollo days, of course. The Orion spacecraft is bigger and heavier than those of the past, so it couldn’t be lifted from the sea with a winch. Instead, it was floated into a Navy vessel. But much of the science remains the same, and the lessons of those early space flights still apply. And NASA will continue to learn what it can from the past, as it looks to the future. “You don’t want to reinvent the wheel,” Villarreal says.

The Apollo team was able for example to paint a picture of what makes all this so hard. Assuming the parachutes open correctly, there is still a lot that can complicate the recovery.

“The weather is always the number one factor,” says Master Chief Navy Diver Ryan Crider, who helped organized the Navy’s efforts to pick up the Artemis II astronauts. Storms can roll in and ocean currents can be hard to predict.

Ocean recovery is a complex operation. “Teams have to manage flotation, sea state, capsule drift, communications, swimmer safety, helicopter or ship coordination and the risk of flooding or capsizing if the vehicle is damaged or not stabilized quickly,” says Les Johnson, former NASA chief technologist at Marshall Space Flight Center.

NASA and the Navy practice for the worst possible conditions. “We try to mimic the most strenuous and stressful situations,” Crider says. “That way, if we do run into rough weather — rough seas, winds, rain, anything like that — it’s not something that we haven’t seen before.”

Much of the practice takes place in the Navy’s Neutral Buoyancy Lab at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where NASA engineers offer step-by-step guidance. “This is how you hook up the stability collar. This is how you hook up the harness,” Crider says. “You learn in a controlled environment how to do everything safely.”

Then they make it less safe. “They will add waves to the situation to make it a little bit more difficult. We’ll turn off the lights,” he says. And when the lab training is done, “We actually go out on a naval vessel and pull a training capsule out, and we do multiple iterations of release and recovery over a five- to seven-day period. That puts us in an actual real-world situation.”

Bringing in the experts

To ensure success, NASA brings scientific expertise to the table.

That starts with “anybody who’s knowledgeable about Orion vehicle,” Villarreal says. Then there are the parachute experts, the weather experts, engineers to deliver the live video feeds that will inform the recovery — or the rescue, should things get tricky.

“We get the Department of War to give us their [plan]: If we have a boat that fails, this is what we’re going to do,” she says. “It’s a combined effort. It takes multiple meetings discussing what could go wrong, and then we all have to agree on the plan.”

In fact, communication and coordination were a big part of what drove the successful Artemis II recovery. “Any time you have a mission of this magnitude, with all of these different organizations coming together for one cause, it can be difficult for everyone to get on the same page,” Crider says.

In training, “we learn how to speak that same language, we learn the same terminology, and we learn how to work with each other to make sure that the mission is successful,” he says.

Practice pays off

On the day Artemis II returned to Earth, Villarreal was with the Navy dive team abord the USS John P. Murtha in the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of California. “We were in communication with Houston. We could hear everything that was going on from the vehicle and the crew,” she says. The weather was perfect, and everything went according to plan. Villarreal watched the video feeds as the parachutes deployed and the spacecraft touched down successfully on the water. “That was such a great moment for us,” she says. “I was very happy to see everything going so well.” The successful Artemis II mission sets the stage for the future of lunar exploration. And the insights gleaned during the Apollo missions half a century ago will continue to inform NASA’s approach.

item.title: What is Artemis II? - National Air and Space Museum
item.description:
Soon, four astronauts will launch on a mission to the vicinity of the Moon for the first time in over 50 years. The mission, called Artemis II, is the second mission — and first crewed mission — of NASA’s Artemis program. NASA is currently targeting Wednesday, April 1, 2026 for the launch. The April 1 launch window opens at 6:24 pm and lasts 120 minutes. NASA has also identified additional launch windows between April 2 and April 6.

Here’s what to expect from the Artemis II mission.

This banner hanging on a fence at Launch Complex 39B was signed by NASA employees and contractors involved in the Artemis II mission.

The 10-day Artemis II mission will fly around the Moon and is considered a test flight of NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems (the systems involved in launching and recovery rockets and spacecraft), the SLS rocket, and the Orion spacecraft.

As a follow-up mission to the uncrewed Artemis I mission in 2022, this crewed mission will allow NASA to flight test Orion’s life-support systems with astronauts on board. This is essential as NASA intends to send astronauts on longer-duration missions as the Artemis program goes on.

Unlike the Apollo program, which launched crews of three, the Artemis program will feature a crew of four astronauts: commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch, and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen. This historic crew features many "firsts." Click on their names to learn more about each of their careers.

Want to learn more about the crew? Check out this blog and keep an eye out for blogs about each of the astronauts in the coming weeks.

When comparing the Artemis program with NASA’s first Moon landing program, Apollo, the closest analog for Artemis II is Apollo 8. Much like Artemis II, Apollo was the first mission in the Apollo program (and in fact, ever) to send humans to the Moon. One major difference between Apollo 8 and Artemis II, however, is that while Apollo 8 orbited the Moon, Artemis II will fly around the Moon but not enter lunar orbit.

Artemis II is anticipated to break Apollo 13’s record (248,655 miles) for the farthest distance humans have traveled from Earth. The Artemis II Orion spacecraft will travel over 4,000 miles beyond the Moon as it flies a loop around the Moon’s far side.

An Orion spacecraft will transport the Artemis II astronauts to the vicinity of the Moon and back. It is capsule-shaped like the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo spacecrafts and seats four astronauts.

Orion has been in development for over 20 years, originally part of an earlier lunar exploration program called Constellation. The crew of Artemis II named their Orion spacecraft Integrity to honor the trust among the people who are bringing this mission to life. The name is also a reference to the massive effort to integrate more than 300,000 individual components into a single spacecraft by teams working across the world.

The Artemis II mission will launch using the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. SLS, which launched for the first time in November 2022 during the Artemis I mission, can launch astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft and cargo into space. This heavy-lift launch vehicle was developed using a combination of components from the Space Shuttle program (specifically solid rocket boosters and RS-25 engines) and new technology.

SLS is one of the most powerful rockets to ever launch, providing 8.8 million pounds of thrust (that’s 15% more thrust than the Saturn V Moon rocket). It is powered by two solid rocket boosters (white) and a core stage (orange) with four RS-25 engines. Two minutes after launch, the solid rocket boosters will separate from the core stage and fall back to Earth, splashing into the ocean. (While the Space Shuttle’s solid rocket boosters were reusable, SLS’s are not, and NASA will not be recovering these solid rocket boosters from the ocean.) The core stage will separate from the Orion spacecraft eight minutes after launch (this happens shortly after “main engine cut off,” or MECO). The core stage will reenter the atmosphere over the Pacific Ocean.

Flight Day 1: Artemis II will begin to fly around the Earth, first in low-Earth orbit and then into a high elliptical orbit. While flying around the Earth, the crew will conduct a 23-hour checkout of the Orion spacecraft – this allows them to test the system while they are still close by the Earth in case any unexpected issues arise. This will include an opportunity for the crew to pilot the spacecraft in manual mode.

Flight Day 2: Orion’s main engine will conduct a trans-lunar injection burn, which sets Orion on its path toward the Moon. This burn also puts the spacecraft on its figure-eight free-return trajectory, which means that the Moon’s gravity will eventually guide the Orion spacecraft back to the Earth even without onboard propulsion. This provides a safeguard should Orion experience engine failure.

Flight Days 3-5: Orion and its crew continue on their journey towards the Moon, entering the "lunar sphere of influence" on Day 5.

Flight Day 6: Orion spacecraft Integrity performs a lunar flyby and conducts both its closest approach to the Moon and its furthest distance from Earth. During the lunar flyby, the crew will make observations and take photos of the far side of the Moon.

Flight Day 7-9: Orion spacecraft leaves the “lunar sphere of influence” and begins its journey back to Earth, which includes the first two return trajectory correction burns.

Flight Day 10: Orion performs its final return trajectory correction burn and the crew prepares for reentry, conducting the reentry checklist. The Orion crew module and service module separate. The Orion spacecraft reenters Earth’s atmosphere and splashes down in the Pacific Ocean with the help of three main parachutes. A U.S. Navy ship will recover Integrity and the crew, welcoming them back to Earth.

Like the great space missions that came before it, Artemis II has an official mission patch that will be worn by the crew on the sleeves of their Orion Crew Survival System spacesuits. The patch designates the mission AII, using the roman numeral for 2 to also evoke the visual of the word “All.” It’s a common refrain amongst the crew and other mission support staff at NASA that this mission is “an endeavor of discovery that seeks to explore for all and by all."

The red line that helps form the A and swirls around the Moon and Earth is representative of the mission’s flight path, which includes the spacecraft flying around both our home planet and its only natural satellite. The depiction of the Earth and the Moon on the path can also be seen as an artistic variation on Apollo 8’s famous "Earthrise" photo, linking that historic mission of the 1960s to this modern-day Moon mission of the 2020s.
